strengths: The design-based formalization of delayed outcomes — treating both event time and outcome value as fixed potential outcomes — is a clean and well-motivated framework that avoids strong superpopulation/tail-modeling assumptions that would be violated by nonstationarity and staggered entry in online experiments.

Theorem 4.4 gives an elegant, exact necessary-and-sufficient characterization of which augmentations preserve the martingale property under the single-arm filtration (activate at event time, remain constant thereafter). This is a nontrivial and practically useful result enabling variance reduction (e.g., via a running-mean augmentation) while preserving anytime-validity.

The negative result (Lemma 4.7 + Proposition 4.8) that the treatment-effect error process is not a martingale under any filtration is a genuine conceptual contribution, cleanly connecting the sequential impossibility to the classical unestimable cross-covariance term in fixed-sample design-based inference (Remark 4.11 draws this analogy nicely).

Proposition 4.12 provides a rigorous asymptotic comparison showing the union bound can be strictly tighter than the naive variance upper bound under asymmetric arrival rates, which is a non-obvious and useful practical insight, and is also illustrated empirically in Figure 2.

The paper includes both a controlled simulation (with realistic nonstationary hazard/shock structure and a documented pull-forward effect) verifying coverage properties of IPW and event-time AIPW estimators, and a real-world case study (software canary OOM monitoring) with a thoughtful comparison to an existing Poisson-process-based competing method (Lindon & Kallus, 2025), highlighting the practical advantage of avoiding a Poisson/proportional-hazards assumption.

Proofs in the appendix are detailed and appear technically careful (martingale verification, strong invariance principle argument, variance-estimator martingale property, asymptotic equivalence of V and V-hat).
weaknesses: The confidence sequences are only asymptotically valid (relying on a strong approximation/invariance principle as Vt(w)→∞), yet the paper's framing and title emphasize 'anytime-valid inference' without sufficiently foregrounding this asymptotic caveat outside the theorem statements; readers could overestimate the strength of the guarantees relative to the exact nonasymptotic confidence sequences typical in this literature (e.g., Howard et al., 2021; Ham et al., 2022).

The reward-process model rit(w) = yi(w)1[ti(w) ≤ t] handles only a single delayed event per unit; the paper does not address recurring/multiple events per unit, which limits the generality of the claimed 'ubiquitous' delayed-outcome setting (e.g., repeated purchases, recurring crashes) even though the abstract and motivation suggest broad applicability.

Empirical validation is limited to a single synthetic DGP with a fixed set of hand-chosen parameters (Dataset 5.1) for the coverage table; there is no systematic sensitivity analysis over degrees of nonstationarity, censoring severity, sample size, or covariate informativeness, which would strengthen confidence in the generality of the coverage and tightness claims.

The augmentation strategy explored is limited to the running mean; the paper does not explore or compare richer covariate-based augmentations (despite motivating access to covariates Xi), leaving the practical variance-reduction potential only partially demonstrated.

The real-data case study, while illustrative, has no ground truth, so it cannot corroborate coverage guarantees empirically; it mainly demonstrates qualitative agreement in point estimates with the Poisson-based competitor, without a rigorous quantitative comparison of interval widths or detection speed across replications.

The asymptotic tightness result comparing the union bound to the variance upper bound (Proposition 4.12) requires idealized asymptotic regimes (V0 = o(V1), V→∞) and constant per-unit propensity; practical guidance on when this benefit materializes in finite, moderately asymmetric samples is only shown for one example (Figure 2) rather than characterized more generally.
